final_proof:
Let \(p_k=\Pr(X=k)\) and \(q_k=\Pr(Y=k)\) for \(k\in\mathbb N\). We assign probability zero to any natural number outside the range of the relevant random variable. Because \(X\) and \(Y\) are natural-number-valued, their probability generating functions are
\[
\Pi_X(s)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb N}p_k s^k,
\qquad
\Pi_Y(s)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb N}q_k s^k.
\]
For every \(s\in[-1,1]\), both series converge absolutely, since
\[
\sum_{k\in\mathbb N}p_k|s|^k\leq\sum_{k\in\mathbb N}p_k=1,
\]
and likewise \(\sum q_k|s|^k\leq1\).

Suppose first that \(p_k=q_k\) for every \(k\in\mathbb N\). The two absolutely convergent series then have identical terms, so \(\Pi_X(s)=\Pi_Y(s)\) for every \(s\in[-1,1]\).

Conversely, suppose that \(\Pi_X(s)=\Pi_Y(s)\) for every \(s\in[-1,1]\). Assume for contradiction that \(p_k\ne q_k\) for some \(k\). By the well-ordering principle, there is a least \(m\in\mathbb N\) such that \(p_m\ne q_m\). Set \(a_k=p_k-q_k\). For every \(s\in(0,1)\), equality of the generating functions and the minimality of \(m\) imply
\[
0=\sum_{k\in\mathbb N}a_k s^k
=s^m\left(a_m+\sum_{k>m}a_k s^{k-m}\right).
\]
Since \(s^m>0\), we may cancel it. Hence
\[
|a_m|
=\left|\sum_{k>m}a_k s^{k-m}\right|
\leq\sum_{k>m}|a_k|s^{k-m}
\leq s\sum_{k>m}(p_k+q_k)
\leq2s.
\]
Here we used \(k-m\geq1\), so \(s^{k-m}\leq s\), and \(|p_k-q_k|\leq p_k+q_k\). The inequality \(|a_m|\leq2s\) holds for every \(s\in(0,1)\); letting \(s\downarrow0\) gives \(|a_m|=0\), contradicting \(p_m\ne q_m\). Thus \(p_k=q_k\) for every \(k\in\mathbb N\).

Therefore \(\Pi_X(s)=\Pi_Y(s)\) for all \(s\in[-1,1]\) if and only if \(\Pr(X=k)=\Pr(Y=k)\) for every \(k\in\mathbb N\).
